Hidebound

HYDE-bound · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Hidebound is rigidly attached to old ways and unwilling to accept new ideas.

The hidebound committee rejected every proposal that didn't match how things had always been done.

Worked Example

The hidebound principal refused to even consider a four-day school week, insisting the schedule had worked fine since 1975.

Hidebound describes a person, group, or institution so attached to old habits that they refuse to seriously consider anything new, even good ideas.

How Hidebound Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

rigid

rigid: unwilling to change or adapt

hidebound-thinking

hidebound-thinking: narrow and inflexible in outlook

Antonyms

progressive

progressive: favoring new ideas and change

flexible

flexible: willing to adapt and adjust

How Strong Is It? — cautious → hidebound → dogmatic

cautious vs. hidebound

cautious vs. hidebound: Being cautious about a new idea still leaves room to eventually accept it.

dogmatic vs. hidebound

dogmatic vs. hidebound: A dogmatic person clings to a belief as absolute truth, an even more rigid stance than simply being hidebound.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of hidebound.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — hide

root — hide: an animal's skin (Old English (hyd))

root — bound

root — bound: tightly fastened (Old English (bunden))

Put it together

Put it together: hide ("skin") + bound ("tightly fastened") = originally describing cattle so starved their skin stuck tight to their ribs.

Where it comes from

Where it comes from: There is no classical root here -- hidebound is simply two everyday English words, hide (an animal's skin) and bound (tightly fastened), joined together. It first described starving cattle whose skin was stuck fast to their ribs, and only later people whose minds are just as tightly fastened to old ideas.

Word Building

Word Choice

Hidebound almost always describes an attitude or institution -- a stubborn refusal to consider new ideas -- rather than a single rigid rule or structure, which is closer to what Ossified describes.
